name: Triangles
kicker: Three sides, three angles · Angles add up to 180° on a flat surface
dates: Angle-sum proof in Euclid’s Elements, c. 300 BCE
briefing: A triangle is the simplest polygon: three straight sides, three corners, and three angles that always add up to 180 degrees on a flat surface. Triangles are sorted by their sides (equilateral, isosceles, or scalene) and by their angles (acute, right, or obtuse), and the Pythagorean theorem works only for right triangles. Engineers build bridges and towers from triangles because, unlike a square, a triangle cannot be pushed out of shape without changing the length of a side.
answerHtml: triangles (accept specific kinds, such as equilateral triangles; prompt on polygons or shapes)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Frank Morley discovered in 1899 that, in any one of these shapes, the angle trisectors nearest each side meet at the corners of a smaller, equilateral one. The point where the three angle bisectors of one of these shapes meet is the center of its inscribed circle.
tossups.r: Each of these shapes has three sides. For 10 points, name these polygons whose three interior angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The Babylonian clay tablet Plimpton 322, made around 1800 BCE, contains columns of numbers that come from whole-number side lengths of right-angled examples of these shapes. In those examples, the side across from the right angle is the longest side, called the hypotenuse.
tossups.r: The Pythagorean theorem applies to right examples of these shapes. For 10 points, name these three-sided polygons.

tossups.p: Franz Reuleaux [“roo-LOH”] names a rounded version of the equilateral one of these shapes that has the same width in every direction, like a circle. Drill bits shaped that way can drill holes that are almost square.
tossups.r: Equilateral examples of these shapes have three 60-degree angles. For 10 points, name these polygons with three sides.

tossups.p: Wacław Sierpiński [“VAHTS-wahf sher-PEEN-skee”] names a fractal made by splitting one of these shapes into four smaller copies and removing the middle one, over and over. The same pattern appears when the odd numbers in the number arrangement named for Blaise Pascal are shaded.
tossups.r: Each one has three sides. For 10 points, name these shapes, which can be equilateral, isosceles, or scalene.

tossups.p: Viviani’s theorem says that from any point inside an equilateral one of these shapes, the distances to the three sides add up to its height. The Fermat point of one of these shapes is the spot with the smallest total distance to its three corners.
tossups.r: They have three sides. For 10 points, name these polygons whose area equals one-half times base times height.

tossups.p: Karl Feuerbach [“FOY-er-bahk”] proved that a circle passing through nine special points of one of these shapes touches the circle inscribed inside it. Those nine points include the midpoints of the shape’s sides and the feet of its altitudes.
tossups.r: An equilateral one of these shapes has three equal sides. For 10 points, name these shapes whose angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter of one of these shapes always lie on a line named for Leonhard Euler, but the incenter usually does not. The centroid, where the three medians meet, is the balance point of one of these shapes.
tossups.r: These shapes can be acute, right, or obtuse. For 10 points, name these three-sided polygons.

tossups.p: Heron of Alexandria gave a formula for the area of one of these shapes that uses only its three side lengths. Thales [“THAY-leez”] is credited with showing that if one of these shapes has all three corners on a circle and one side is a diameter, the angle opposite that side is a right angle.
tossups.r: The area of one of these shapes is half its base times its height. For 10 points, name these polygons with three sides.

tossups.p: M. C. Escher’s print _Waterfall_ uses an impossible version of this shape that was popularized by Lionel and Roger Penrose. On the surface of a sphere, the three angles of this shape add up to more than 180 degrees.
tossups.r: On a flat surface, they add up to exactly 180 degrees. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: A theorem credited to Napoleon Bonaparte says that if equilateral versions of this shape are built outward on the sides of any one of them, their centers form another equilateral one. The first proposition of Euclid’s _Elements_ constructs an equilateral one.
tossups.r: This shape can be acute, right, or obtuse. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: Knowing two sides of this shape and an angle that is not between them can describe two different examples of it, which is why “SSA” cannot prove that two of them are congruent. The shortcuts SSS, SAS, and ASA do work.
tossups.r: Two of these with matching angles are similar. For 10 points, name this polygon whose three angles add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: Three of the five Platonic solids, the tetrahedron, the octahedron, and the icosahedron, have faces in this shape. Equilateral versions of this shape are one of only three regular polygons that can tile a flat surface with no gaps, along with squares and hexagons.
tossups.r: Its area is one-half times base times height. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon.

tossups.p: The name of one type of this shape comes from Greek words meaning “equal legs,” and Euclid’s proof that its two base angles are equal was nicknamed the “bridge of donkeys.” Bridge trusses are built from this shape because it is rigid.
tossups.r: It is the polygon with the fewest sides. For 10 points, name this shape, which can be equilateral, isosceles, or scalene.

tossups.p: One special right example of this shape has angles of 30, 60, and 90 degrees and sides in the ratio 1 to the square root of 3 to 2. Any exterior angle of this shape equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.
tossups.r: This shape has three sides. For 10 points, name this polygon whose three angles always add up to 180 degrees.

tossups.p: The name of the branch of math that studies the sides and angles of this shape comes from the Greek words for it and for “measure.” According to an inequality named for this shape, the lengths of any two of its sides must add up to more than the third.
tossups.r: Its angles add up to 180 degrees. For 10 points, name this three-sided polygon, whose right-angled versions obey the Pythagorean theorem.

clues.t: A polygon with three sides, three vertices, and three angles; the polygon with the fewest sides
On a flat surface, its three interior angles always add up to 180 degrees
By sides: equilateral (all three equal), isosceles (at least two equal), or scalene (none equal)
By angles: acute (all under 90°), right (one exactly 90°), or obtuse (one over 90°)
Area = one-half × base × height
Right ones obey the Pythagorean theorem, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse
Equilateral ones have three 60° angles, making them the regular three-sided polygon
Any two sides added together must be longer than the third side (an inequality named for this shape)
Congruence shortcuts SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS work, but SSA does not; two with matching angles are similar, with sides in proportion
They are rigid, which is why bridge trusses and bicycle frames are built from them
Heron’s formula finds the area from the three side lengths, using half the perimeter (the semiperimeter)
Centers: centroid (medians), circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors), incenter (angle bisectors), orthocenter (altitudes)
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two interior angles that are not next to it
Special right ones: 30-60-90 (sides 1 : √3 : 2) and 45-45-90 (sides 1 : 1 : √2)
The centroid, circumcenter, and orthocenter always lie on the Euler line; the incenter usually does not
The nine-point circle passes through the side midpoints and the feet of the altitudes; Feuerbach showed it touches the inscribed circle
Napoleon’s theorem: build equilateral ones outward on the sides of any one, and their centers form another equilateral one
Morley’s theorem (discovered 1899): in any one, the angle trisectors nearest each side meet at the corners of an equilateral one
Viviani’s theorem: in an equilateral one, distances from any inside point to the sides add up to its height; the Fermat point minimizes total distance to the corners
Wacław Sierpiński’s 1915 fractal removes the middle one of four smaller copies, again and again
The Reuleaux shape, a rounded version of the equilateral one, has the same width in every direction
An impossible version, popularized by Lionel and Roger Penrose, appears in M. C. Escher’s print _Waterfall_
On a sphere, the angles add up to more than 180°; in hyperbolic geometry, to less than 180°
Thales’ theorem: if all three corners are on a circle and one side is a diameter, the angle opposite it is a right angle
The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 (about 1800 BCE) holds numbers from whole-number sides of right ones
Equilateral ones tile a flat surface (as squares and hexagons do) and form the faces of the tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron
“Isosceles” is Greek for “equal legs”; Euclid’s proof that its base angles are equal is the pons asinorum, “bridge of donkeys”
The math of their sides and angles is named from Greek words for this shape and “measure”

trap.title: Any shape or one kind?
trap.body: Some tossups want one specific kind: equilateral (all sides equal), isosceles (at least two equal sides), scalene (no equal sides), or right (one 90° angle). On those, plain “triangle” may earn only a prompt, so be ready to add the type. Other tossups want the Pythagorean theorem, which works only for right ones, or Pascal’s triangle, which is a pattern of numbers rather than a shape.
trap.fix: Listen to the giveaway. If it says “three-sided polygon” with clues true of every one (angles add up to 180°, area is one-half × base × height), say “triangle.” If it gives a defining detail like “all three sides equal” or “one 90-degree angle,” name that kind.
trap.line: Real answer line: triangles (accept specific kinds, such as equilateral triangles; prompt on polygons or shapes)
